title: A Problem History of Distributed Coordination

fieldQualification.rationale: Backend engineering is a profession; distributed systems is the recognized research field matching the learner's interest in coordination under scale and failure.
recognitionEvidence: A durable research community publishes and evaluates contributions at venues including SOSP and OSDI.
The field has established problem families, formal models, empirical methods, and unresolved research questions.

doctoralOutcome: Evaluate competing system designs and formulate a defensible research question.
abstract: This review traces how distributed coordination changed as scale and failure exposed the limits of earlier designs.
scope: The tutorial covers foundational designs through the first scalable architecture and excludes later product-specific variants.
thesis: Progress came from changing the unit of coordination rather than optimizing the original mechanism.
reviewMethod: Works are selected for their role as baseline, turning point, critique, or synthesis; exact citations are verified against primary sources.
researchQuestions: Which limitation forced the field to change its coordination model?
What evidence justified the turning point?

apprenticeshipSequence: Trace one coordination behavior from specification through implementation and test.
Reproduce a failure and instrument the responsible subsystem.
Modify the mechanism and evaluate the resulting tradeoff.
researchPractice.frontierContribution: Derive and evaluate a new coordination mechanism from a historically persistent limitation.

chapterPlan.title: The coordination crisis
chapterPlan.transitionSummary: Scale and failure turn central coordination from a simplifying assumption into the field's binding limitation.

chapterPlan.title: Coordination under weaker assumptions
chapterPlan.transitionSummary: Researchers expose and relax the timing and failure assumptions inherited from the first distributed protocols.

chapters.title: The coordination crisis
chapters.historicalSituation: Early systems optimized for small, trusted environments.
chapters.centralProblem: The original coordination mechanism failed as participation and latency increased.

priorApproaches.name: Central coordination
priorApproaches.contribution: Established a simple and inspectable baseline.
priorApproaches.limitation: A single coordinator became a bottleneck and failure domain.

turningPoint.name: Distributed coordination
turningPoint.idea: Move agreement from one coordinator to a protocol among participants.
turningPoint.whyItWorked: The protocol made failure assumptions explicit and distributed responsibility.

chapters.methodAndMechanism: Participants exchange evidence and advance only after a defined agreement threshold.
chapters.evidenceAndEvaluation: The approach is judged through safety arguments, liveness conditions, and controlled failure experiments.
limitationsAndDebates: The model assumes bounded forms of failure.
downstreamInfluence: New research studied coordination with adversarial participants.
chapters.doctoralSynthesis: The learner can explain why the turning point changed the failure model rather than merely improving speed.
chapters.primaryArtifactInvestigation: Trace the agreement threshold from its specification into source code and reproduce one controlled failure using the system tests.
learningTasks: Reconstruct the causal transition without notes.
Design an experiment that distinguishes the two approaches.
chapters.masteryGate: Defend which assumptions are necessary for safety and identify one researchable limitation.

works.role: Turning-point work used to test HTML escaping and source labels.

crossChapterSynthesis: The transition replaced implicit trust in a coordinator with explicit assumptions distributed across a protocol.
openProblems: How can the protocol retain its guarantees with weaker timing assumptions?

doctoralRubric.standard: Explains why each approach emerged, what it solved, and which new problem it exposed.
